## Decisions, locked

1. **Give the thesis talk**, not the dashboard-patterns talk. The dashboard stays
   as the case study.
2. **Stay in the session.** Don't move to "Late-breaking AI."
3. **No three-pillar framing.** One spine sentence, six acts.
4. **Never name Thariq** or reference the HTML post. Make the HTML case yourself.
5. **The dashboard gets 6 protected minutes, mid-deck** — not 3 at the end.
6. **Rebuild the entanglement figure** — the nested-box version had a conceptual
   bug, not a layout problem.

---

## The claim

::: {.verdict}
**Quarto's separation of content from format was built as a discipline for
humans. It turns out to be a safety mechanism for machines — and now that the
machines are doing the writing, it's the cheap path instead of the expensive
one.**
:::

Nothing in that sentence is a fact about Quarto the room doesn't know. All of it
is a reframe of what those facts are now *for*. That's what an idea talk is.

**Spine sentence, said 3× from the stage:**

> **Agents should write the source, not the artifact.**

A repeated *claim* anchors better than three nouns, because a claim can be
argued and a noun can't. Note what it does **not** say: "put your content in data
files." It says hand me the source. Everything else follows.

---

## What's actually novel

The honest starting point: **strip the agents out and this talk is the Quarto
elevator pitch.** The room grants content/format separation, reproducibility, and
one-source-many-formats before you open your mouth. The novelty was never
supposed to live in a claim about Quarto — it lives in claims about the
*situation Quarto is now in.*

### 1. The economics inverted {.unnumbered}

For fifteen years reproducibility was a **discipline** — something you do for
future-you at a cost to present-you. Everyone in that room believes in it, and
everyone in that room has a folder of ad-hoc scripts they never turned into a
`.qmd`, because the tax was real.

Agents removed the tax. Writing the source is now cheaper than producing the
artifact. **The virtuous path became the lazy path.** That's a claim about
incentives, it became true about eighteen months ago, and nobody has heard it.

**This is where the token experiment belongs** — not as a benchmark, but as the
*receipt*. 7.2× isn't a bonus stat; it's the evidence the incentive flipped. That
also fixes the worry that tokens steal the headline: they stop being a lesser
second claim and become proof of the first.

### 2. Prose gets *located*; data gets *derived* {.unnumbered}

::: {.warn}
**Revised — the earlier version of this overreached.** "It's sentences now, not
numbers" implied you should extract prose into data files. Nobody writes that
way, and the room would rightly reject it. The handwriting sheet works because
those sentences genuinely *are* data — a list of items to typeset, more parameter
than paragraph. **Don't generalize from it.**
:::

The defensible version has two tiers, and both are things a fused artifact
denies you:

| | Where it lives | What you get |
|---|---|---|
| **Prose** | in the `.qmd` | an address — a line number, and a **diff** you can read |
| **Values that must be exact** | in data + code | not just locatable, **recomputed** — never typed |

What's genuinely new here isn't extraction. It's that **diffability became a
correctness mechanism rather than a convenience.** Pre-LLM, a human wrote the
prose and the risk surface was the numbers — which knitr solved in 2012. Post-LLM
the prose is generated too, and the answer for prose isn't a CSV, it's
addressability. That's the part the room hasn't thought through.

Say it as: *"The move isn't extract everything. It's stop asking for the
artifact."*

### 3. The belief–behavior gap {.unnumbered}

The empirical bet: **nearly all of them believe in source-over-artifact, and a
minority ask agents for a `.qmd`.** They use Quarto for their own analysis, then
open a chat window and ask for the finished thing, because that's what the chat
window invites. The habit didn't transfer.

That gap *is* the talk. Naming it out loud is also the **defense against "we
already knew that"** — raise the objection before the audience can:

> *"Everything I'm about to tell you, you already believe. I want to know why
> almost none of us do it."*

Instead of thinking *I knew that*, they think *…why don't I do that?*

### 4. Render is a verification loop the agent can close {.unnumbered}

The sharpest thing in the talk, and the strongest answer to the HTML objection.

An agent writing HTML **cannot tell whether it's wrong** — no compile step,
malformed output still renders as *something*, the failure is silent. An agent
writing a `.qmd` gets a loud deterministic error (bad cross-ref, failed chunk,
invalid YAML) and can **read it and fix it without you in the loop.**

Not "Quarto is reproducible." Rather: **documents just got a compile step, and
they got it exactly when their authors became probabilistic.**

State the limit on the slide — render passing ≠ analysis correct, same as
compiling ≠ correct. Ten seconds, and it buys more credibility than anything else
in the deck.

---

## Why six acts and not three pillars

::: {.quiet}
The act table lives in `CLAUDE.md`. This is why it's shaped that way.
:::

**A benefits list has no tension.** Every one of "Correctness / Efficiency /
Trust" is a good property of Quarto, and a room that already loves Quarto grants
all three for free. The structure itself produces the recap feeling. Taxonomies
enumerate; they don't argue. Nothing is ever at stake on a pillar slide.

**Correctness and Trust also aren't siblings** — Trust is the *feeling produced
by* correctness plus verifiability. What was loaded into "Trust" is actually
*verifiability*, a mechanism, while Correctness is an outcome. Different kinds of
thing in the same row, and the room feels the mush without being able to name it.

The three ideas survive as **earned consequences** instead:

| Old pillar | Becomes | Where |
|---|---|---|
| Correctness | the **problem** | Acts 1–2, as tension and release |
| Efficiency | the **turn** | Act 3, as the surprise |
| Trust | the **mechanism** | Act 5, merged with the HTML objection |

**Three things the act structure buys:**

- **It has a turn.** Act 3 is a genuine surprise — braced for a worthiness
  argument, the audience gets an argument about cost. Talks get quoted for turns,
  never for taxonomies.
- **It merges the HTML objection with the verification point,** which were doing
  overlapping work. The concession now has a punchline, and it saves ~2 minutes.
- **It protects the dashboard.** Six minutes, mid-deck, where overrun can't reach
  it. If you run long you cut a concession, not your most concrete material.

**Recurring anchor:** the transforming figure, not a word slide. It *advances*
instead of repeating, and the design effort is already sunk.

---

## The figure: why it was rebuilt

::: {.warn}
**The bug was conceptual.** The old output glyph was an amber box **inside** a
blue box — but containment means the two things are already separate and nested,
which is the visual opposite of entanglement. The concept was being carried by
decoration (ragged edges, a "?" badge) while the *structure* of the picture said
something else. No amount of polish fixes that.
:::

Two compounding problems: boxes-and-arrows-in-a-row is the universal grammar for
**pipeline**, so it read as "here's a workflow" when the thesis is "here are two
things fused"; and at 5 clicks with a retargeting arrow there was more motion
than a room can track from row 25.

**The operational definition everything now rests on:**

> Ask of a generated document: **where *is* the sentence?** There's no line of
> anything that *is* it — it's smeared across one probabilistic pass. To change
> it you regenerate everything and hope.
>
> **That's entanglement: the content has no address.** And the fix states itself.

Keep "entanglement" as the label — it's vivid and sticky — but define it with the
pointing test, because *"can you point at it?"* is a question the audience can
apply to their own work immediately.

**The replacement** (`images/entanglement-diagram/weave-figure.qmd`, spec in
`CLAUDE.md`): two stacked rows, one `<use>`d output bar so they're provably
identical, provenance drawn as a thread back to a row in a file. The empty gap in
row 1 is exactly the space Quarto fills in row 2.

**Its job in Act 2 is generalization, not explanation** — the handwriting sheet
already taught the idea. That's an easier job and it justifies a simpler picture.

---

## The HTML section, in your own voice

Naming Thariq is a **net negative**. Conceding to a named rival is only good
rhetoric when the room knows the rival; otherwise you pay exposition to introduce
an opponent, argue their side for them, then rebut — while part of the audience
wonders who that was. It also makes the talk dependent on someone else's post.

The title formula is a genre, not a reference (Wigner 1960 on mathematics, later
reused for data and for RNNs). It carries its own meaning and needs no help.
**Never explain the title.**

::: {.verdict}
Frame it as **the objection, at full strength, in your voice**:

> *"So why not just ask for HTML? Honestly — let me make the case for HTML,
> because it's a good one."*

Rich, structured, immediately viewable, no toolchain, and far better than a wall
of Markdown. Then turn.
:::

Strictly better on four counts: zero exposition cost; you own both sides so the
pushback reads as honesty rather than rivalry; it works whether or not anyone
knows the reference; and it's **the objection a sharp listener is already
forming.** Same move as the Act 1 defusing line — *name the objection first,
every time.*

Keep the throwaway-editors concession as your own honest limit: *"if it's
single-use and disposable, take the HTML."* One sentence, real credibility, no
third party.

## Session context

Session labeled "Dashboards"; the lineup is about **data products**:

| # | Talk | Really about |
|---|---|---|
| **1** | **Unreasonable Effectiveness of Quarto** — *you* | write the source, not the artifact |
| 2 | Tableau Plateau → AI-Ready Data Products — Blake Abbenante | dashboards aren't the end state |
| 3 | Custom Catalogs to Connect Users with Data Products — Malosree Maitra | discoverability for data products |
| 4 | Scaling Reports: Template > Package > App — Jadey Ryan & Tanya Shapiro | escalating abstraction |

The through-line is **the artifact is not the thing — the system that produces it
is.** That's your thesis, and you're first. You are the session's opening
statement, not its outlier.

Two consequences: **you don't owe this room a dashboard tutorial** (nobody else
is giving one) — keep the case study because it's your best *evidence*, not a
debt. And **use the phrase "data product."** It's the session's shared vocabulary
and it costs nothing.

**Hand off at the close.** Generous to the co-speakers, makes the session cohere,
and retroactively makes your talk its foundation:

> *"You're about to hear three more talks about building data products. Watch for
> the same move in each — the artifact is never the thing. The thing is whatever
> produces it."*

<p class="quiet">On not moving to "Late-breaking AI": it would invert your
scarcity position — you're currently the only person in your session making an
agent-correctness argument, and "we just heard that twenty minutes ago" is worse
than "we already knew that." The session is also empty and unannounced, and the
audience is wrong: your belief–behavior argument needs people who hold the belief
but not the habit, which is a builder room, not an AI-news room. The existence of
that session and your absence from it is the best possible outcome for the
novelty problem.</p>

  benchmark — the cold open already tells that story, this just prices it.
- **The four dashboard placeholders** — 2 patterns, 2 pitfalls. Most-remembered
  slides in any practitioner talk, and now load-bearing.
